00:03.000–00:04.000 — Voice continues: “Nirvana is when everything the mind makes comes to a stop.”

00:04.000–00:05.000 — Voice continues: “The letting go of everything carried, the thirst ends.”

00:07.000–00:08.000 — Voice pauses briefly. No speech. Silence.

00:10.000–00:11.000 — Voice continues: “Now when a fire burns, it does so with the help of firewood.”

00:11.000–00:12.000 — Voice continues: “When a fire is burning, if someone were to ask us, ‘What is burning? What shall we say as a reply?’”

00:13.000–00:14.000 — Voice continues: “The truth of the matter is that the wood burns because of the fire, and the fire burns because of the wood.”

00:14.000–00:15.000 — Voice continues: “So it seems we already have here a case of relatedness of this to that, ida-paccayata.”

00:15.000–00:16.000 — Voice continues: “This itself shows that there is a very deep significance in the fire simile.”

s2.text:
00:00–00:02 — A single, sustained, high-pitched electronic tone, pure sine wave, centered in the stereo field, no speech, no background noise.

00:02–00:05 — A female voice begins speaking, clear and natural, mid-sentence: “Why don’t I see Nirvana right now?”

00:05–00:13 — A male voice responds, calm and measured, mid-sentence: “You do not see Nirvana right now because you imagine a seer and a world, and neither is there.”

00:13–00:23 — The same male voice continues, mid-sentence: “What is called manana is the imagining in egoistic terms, imparting reality to illusory things.”

00:23–00:31 — Male voice continues, mid-sentence: “Only looking is there, nothing worth looking at. Only a seeing is there, nothing to be seen.”

00:31–00:40 — Male voice continues, mid-sentence: “The law of dependent arising is already implicated. There is therefore no seer apart from the phenomenon of seeing, according to the Tathagata.”

00:40–00:48 — Male voice continues, mid-sentence: “Samsara is a whirlpool as far as the ordinary beings caught up in it are concerned.”

00:48–00:55 — Male voice continues, mid-sentence: “Now what about the arhants? How is the idea of this whirlpool presented in the case of the arhants?”

00:55–01:03 — Male voice continues, mid-sentence: “It is simply said that for them there is no whirling round for there to be a designation.”

01:03–01:11 — Male voice continues, mid-sentence: “Pattang tesa nati panyapanaaya. So in their case, there is no whirling round to justify a designation.”

01:11–01:20 — Male voice continues, mid-sentence: “This then is something deeper than the whirlpool itself. The whirlpool can be pointed out because of its activity, but not so easily the emancipated ones.”

01:20–01:28 — Male voice continues, mid-sentence: “And that is why there is so much controversy regarding the nature of the Tathagata.”

01:28–01:37 — Male voice continues, mid-sentence: “The image of the whirlpool in its relation to the emancipated ones is beautifully presented in the following verse from the Culla Vagga of the Udana.”

01:37–01:48 — Male voice continues, mid-sentence: “Achchivatang vyaagani rasam visukka saritana sandati. Chinnam vattangna vattati ese phandu dukkhasam.”

01:48–01:56 — Male voice continues, mid-sentence: “Now, how did the Middle Path, which the Buddha introduced to the world, avoid these two extremes?”

01:56–02:05 — Male voice continues, mid-sentence: “It is by offering a knowledge and vision of things as they are, yatha bhuta nyanadassana, in place of those two views of existence and non-existence.”

02:05–02:14 — Male voice continues, mid-sentence: “In other words, he made known to the world the true knowledge and vision, that name and form is merely an image reflected on consciousness.”

00:00.000 --> 00:02.500: A single, sustained, high-pitched electronic tone, pure sine wave, centered in the stereo field. No speech, no other sounds.

00:02.500 --> 00:03.500: The tone ends abruptly. Silence.

00:03.500 --> 00:06.000: A male voice begins speaking. “What keeps it going?” — clear, mid-range, natural timbre, moderate pace. No background noise.

00:06.000 --> 00:07.000: The first voice ends. Silence.

00:07.000 --> 00:10.000: A second male voice begins. “Thirst keeps it going, impelled by that making it into something, it runs towards the mirage, the gap is ignored.” — slightly lower pitch, deliberate pacing, clear diction.

00:10.000 --> 00:11.000: The second voice ends. Silence.

00:11.000 --> 00:14.000: A third male voice begins. “What impels one to ignore that gap is thirst.” — similar pitch and tone to the second, slightly more resonant, measured delivery.

00:14.000 --> 00:15.000: The third voice ends. Silence.

00:15.000 --> 00:18.000: A fourth male voice begins. “Perception. What impels one to ignore that gap is craving.” — slightly higher pitch than previous, more emphatic on “craving,” clear articulation.

00:18.000 --> 00:19.000: The fourth voice ends. Silence.

00:19.000 --> 00:22.000: A fifth male voice begins. “That desire, that lust, that delight, that craving in form, feeling, perception, preparations, consciousness, which which one is attached and thoroughly attached to it, therefore is one called a being.” — slower, more deliberate, with slight pauses between phrases, slightly lower pitch.

00:22.000 --> 00:23.000: The fifth voice ends. Silence.

00:23.000 --> 00:26.000: A sixth male voice begins. “In this way we can understand the difference between the two words papancha and pamada in respect of the nuances associated with them.” — clear, academic tone, steady pace.

00:26.000 --> 00:27.000: The sixth voice ends. Silence.

00:27.000 --> 00:30.000: A seventh male voice begins. “Commentaries very often explain the term papancha simply as a synonym of craving, conceit and views.” — slightly faster pace, more clipped articulation.

00:30.000 --> 00:31.000: The seventh voice ends. Silence.

00:31.000 --> 00:34.000: An eighth male voice begins. “Tanha, ditti, mana, nyan, etam adi vachanam.” — recites Pali phrase with clear pronunciation, slightly elevated pitch on “etam,” then lowers.

00:00:04.000 --> 00:00:05.000: The male voice continues. “The sense of self is constructed like this: when one looks into a mirror, one suddenly becomes self-conscious.”

00:00:05.000 --> 00:00:06.000: The male voice continues. “Even with no such notion, the moment one looks, one is reminded of it, as if to exclaim, ‘Ah, here I am.’”

00:00:06.000 --> 00:00:07.000: The male voice continues. “Even if one already has no such notion, the moment one looks into a mirror, one is suddenly reminded of it, as if to exclaim, ‘Ah, here I am.’”

00:00:07.000 --> 00:00:08.000: The male voice continues. “This is the gist of what Ven. Punnamantani Putta is trying to put across through this discourse.”

00:00:08.000 --> 00:00:09.000: The male voice continues. “This shows that the conceit ‘I’ arises due to the five grasping groups.”

00:00:09.000 --> 00:00:10.000: The male voice continues. “The gist of this paragraph is that the non-manifestative consciousness, which is infinite and all-lustrous, is free from the qualities associated with any of the concepts in the list, such as the earthiness of earth and the wateriness of water.”

00:00:10.000 --> 00:00:11.000: The male voice continues. “That is to say, it is not under the influence, it does not partake of them, ‘anubhutam.’”

00:00:11.000 --> 00:00:12.000: The male voice continues. “Whatever nature the word attributes to these concepts, whatever reality they invest it with, that is not registered in this non-manifestative consciousness.”

00:00:12.000 --> 00:00:13.000: The male voice continues. “That is why this consciousness is said to be uninfluenced by them.”

00:00–00:02: A single sustained high-pitched tone, likely a musical note or electronic beep, is heard. No speech or other sounds present.

00:02–00:04: A male voice begins speaking, saying: “Nirvana is only attained now, in seeing just the seeing, with no ‘I’ added...”

00:04–00:07: The same male voice continues: “...then it will not carry you, nothing to stand on, nowhere to land, neither here nor there nor in between. This itself is the end of suffering.”

00:07–00:10: The male voice continues: “And when you’re by it, there will be in the seeing just the seeing, in the heard just the heard, in the sense just the sense, in the cognized just the cognized. Then by it you are not by it.”

00:10–00:13: The male voice continues: “And when you’re not by it, you’re not in it. And when by it you’re not in it, then by it you are neither here nor there nor in between. This itself is the end of suffering.”

00:13–00:15: A brief pause. No speech or other sounds.

00:15–00:18: A different male voice begins speaking: “The basic principle in this training seems to be the discipline to stop short at bare awareness. Dite, ditamattang, sutte, sutamattang, etc.”

00:18–00:21: The same voice continues: “The latter half of the discourse seems to indicate what happens when one goes through that training. The entire discourse is a presentation of the triple training of morality, concentration and wisdom in a nutshell.”

00:21–00:24: The same voice continues: “As for a simile, let us take up the razor, which is such a useful requisite in our meditative life.”

00:24–00:26: A comment is added by a different male voice: “I just wanted to explain to those who might not be familiar with it. This is... the Venerable is speaking about the type of razor used in old times and which is still accustomed to be used in the forest tradition, which is like... like... like a long blade and then a handle. And so one has to sharpen it on a stone in order to be able to shave one’s head, which as monastics we have to do very regularly.”

00:26–00:28: The comment ends. A brief pause.

00:28–00:31: The first male voice resumes: “There’s a certain special way in sharpening a razor. With the idea of sharpening the razor, if one grabs it tightly and rubs it on the sharpening stone, it will only become blunt.”

00:31–00:34: The same voice continues: “Paramasana, grasping, grabbing, is something like that. What then is the alternative?”

00:34–00:37: The same voice continues: “A more refined and softer approach is required, as meant by the term sammasana.”

00:37–00:40: The same voice continues: “There’s a proper mode of doing it. One has to hold the razor in a relaxed way, as if one is going to throw it away.”

00:40–00:43: The same voice continues: “One holds it lightly, ready to let go of it at any time, but of course with mindfulness.”
